title: Don't soothe or distract during meltdowns—naming what's hard works better
dek: Two mothers tried a counterintuitive suggestion: name the loss at transitions instead of soothing, distracting, or comforting. After weeks, both their children's door-slamming meltdowns and hair-pulling self-soothing noticeably decreased.
why: This episode is a listener follow-up with no new theory, but real results proving that naming feelings is genuinely effective, not indulgent.
who: For parents experiencing pick-up meltdowns, children who suddenly become fearful, or anyone doubting whether "naming feelings" really works.
skip: The opening thanks for pre-orders and show introduction can be skipped; content begins with the first listener's situation.

points.h: Door-slamming meltdowns emerge within three weeks of school transfer
points.body: One mother noticed her 4-year-old daughter saying goodbye happily at her previous school. After transferring to the same school where the mother teaches, the situation deteriorated within three weeks: first, complaints about the cafeteria being too loud and cold; then crying and chasing to the door; finally kicking, biting, and slamming the glass door. The school has asked the mother to skip early pick-up this week.

points.h: Visibility without access: the harder problem than simple separation
points.body: Janet highlights an unspoken dynamic the mother hadn't articulated: being in the same building as your primary attachment figure but having no access to her is harder than separation for a determined child. The mother confirmed that discussing this openly, plus letting her daughter choose which door to exit through and get a kiss goodbye, noticeably improved pick-ups. Her older sister began helping with classroom tasks.

points.h: Toddlers resort to hair-pulling when family transitions extend for weeks
points.body: A second mother writes that her 21-month-old daughter pulls her hair to self-soothe during frustration, exhaustion, or boredom. The family is managing a life transition that will last another 4–6 weeks. She's already coaching her daughter to say "I'm frustrated," and has tried ice rings, string toys, and pacifiers. But she admits it "really bothers me" to watch.

points.h: Naming the transition's difficulty visibly reduced meltdowns in both families
points.body: Janet gives both mothers identical counsel: speak directly to the hardship ("this change is hard," "you might miss the way things were") rather than instinctively soothing, distracting, or reassuring. The point isn't to elicit an answer—it's to let the child feel witnessed. Both mothers report back: naming the feeling itself noticeably reduced hair-pulling and pick-up meltdowns.

points.h: Parents' language shapes the emotion more than the event does
points.body: Janet raises a subtler mechanism: when a child reacts intensely, anxious parents often label it—"you're scared," "you're angry," "you're so upset you're falling apart"—but the child may have only been startled or surprised, something far milder. Parental language teaches children to inhabit emotions larger than reality warrants.

points.h: Replacing "scared" with specifics lets children approach what they feared
points.body: This mother realized "scared" and "afraid" were nearly her daughter's only emotion vocabulary. Reflecting those words back each time was cementing the fear. She shifted to "that bird startled you" or "that's a loud sound" instead of "you're scared." Her daughter stopped reporting fear as often and began approaching things she'd previously avoided—like walking past the parking lot hand-in-hand instead of asking to be carried.

points.h: When meltdowns are truly intense, the guidance becomes less clear
points.body: One mother raises a question Janet sidestepped: when the reaction is truly intense—shrieking, hard crying—should she still keep it measured ("wow, you really don't like that") while calmly scooping her up, or shift to something weightier? She hasn't yet figured out the right calibration for genuine meltdowns.

points.h: Witnessing and holding space, not fixing: the parent's real job
points.body: Janet's answer: children don't need parents to hit the perfect phrase or diagnose the emotion precisely. Often they need nothing but space to fully release the feeling, with parents ready to pick her up, or not, or simply let her cry on the floor. She frames the role as "present, caring, empathetic, but not here to fix the problem"—something that requires a lifetime of practice.

terms.def: The caregiver a child emotionally relies on most and around whom they release their strongest feelings, usually a parent.

quotes.text: After her, quote, suspension from morning early drop-off for two days, and our conversation about how it was hard to be in the same space as mommy, but not being able to get her, she has had much better drop-offs.
We've been practicing verbalizing I'm frustrated, which is helping a bit, redirecting through things like cold teething rings, pull string toys, her pacifier.

my husband and I just listened to the episode. It was really helpful. We've been more specific in just verbalizing her feelings and experience when she's feeling tired or frustrated. And it's helped a lot with tantrums and the hair pulling has been less.

Your advice to take some of the words our daughter uses, particularly her labeling of everything as scary with a grain of salt was especially invaluable. I realized that scared and afraid were among the relatively few emotion words she knew, and we were probably giving those words even more power by reflecting them back to her so often.
The only piece I'm still unsure about is what to do when her reaction is really intense, when she's genuinely hysterical, screaming and crying and struggling to settle.
We're showing our care and compassion by allowing it to happen and getting comfortable in our role as available, caring, empathetic non-fixers.
It's about us being uncomfortable and wanting to make them better so we don't have to feel out of control or worried or scared.
